strengths: Novel problem identification: Formalizes multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing as a distinct phenomenon with clear mechanisms (intrinsic hallucination + propagation), distinct from single-agent problems

Rigorous analytical foundation: Turn/layer/token-wise attention analyses across 6 models with systematic ablations of 5 token subsets, providing convincing empirical evidence for root causes (62% attention reduction)
Comprehensive experimental validation: 8 benchmarks × 10 models (7B-34B) × 4 MAS structures with consistent 2.4-4.4% improvements and clear ablation studies demonstrating component contributions
Well-motivated method design: Solution directly derives from analytical findings; unimodal token identification and attention reallocation are clearly justified by preceding experiments
Practical applicability: Plug-and-play approach compatible with diverse VLMs, handles Flash-Attention variants via Key-Norm alternative, minimal computational overhead
Strong comparative analysis: Substantially outperforms adapted single-agent methods (34.4% HS score improvement) with systematic comparison across five baseline approaches
Scaling analysis: Larger models (34B+) show greater improvements (>4%), suggesting method unlocks latent potential in stronger baselines
Comprehensive supporting analyses: Token visualization (Figure 4), agent turn impact analysis (Figure 7), hyperparameter sensitivity (Tables 9-11)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Solution combines well-established techniques (attention-based token selection, temperature scaling, lightweight transformer blocks); individual components lack novelty with contribution primarily in their combination
Modest improvements: 2.4-3.8% on main benchmarks and ~4% on hallucination-specific benchmarks are consistent but incremental; improvements diminish for already-strong baselines

Theoretical understanding gaps: Primarily empirical work lacking formal analysis of hallucination propagation dynamics; no theoretical guarantees or mechanistic explanation for why unimodal attention peaks preserve visual information

Questionable HS metric design: Equation 7's sigmoid weighting function appears ad-hoc without principled justification; relies on external GPT-4 judgment introducing noise; not validated independently
Insufficient unimodal token analysis: Demonstrates empirical importance but lacks depth in explaining WHY unimodal tokens are special; no analysis of semantic content captured or causal mechanisms

Experimental design limitations: No baseline of directly passing original images to all agents; circular MAS structure artificially dense; chain length analysis limited to 20 turns; no comparison against image-sharing alternatives

Generalization concerns: Homogeneous model families (LLaVA/Qwen variants); single-image only despite mentioning video support; English-only evaluation; no proprietary models; appendix acknowledges missing 3B/72B parameter experiments

Hyperparameter sensitivity: Three key parameters require tuning (ω, τ, α₁, α₂) without principled setting procedure; Key-Norm alternative shows 0.5-0.6% degradation—non-trivial for claimed improvements

Reproducibility issues: Code unavailable (promised future release); lightweight transformer block underspecified; visual relay token insertion mechanism unclear; some implementation details lack clarity

Weak failure analysis: No systematic investigation of when/why method underperforms; missing analysis of scenario-specific hallucination types and their correlation with attention patterns; limited edge case discussion

strengths: Novel and well-articulated problem formulation distinguishing intrinsic hallucination from hallucination propagation in multi-agent VLM systems
Comprehensive and convincing empirical analysis with turn-wise, layer-wise, and token-wise attention studies across 6 VLMs demonstrating 62% attention reduction in middle layers
Consistent improvements across diverse settings: 8 benchmarks, 4 MAS structures, 10 base models (2.4-4.4% average gains, stronger on challenging benchmarks)
Practical, plug-and-play method design with minimal overhead and compatibility with modern acceleration techniques (Flash-Attention support via Key-Norm alternative)
Well-designed ablation studies with five distinct token subset categories (random, inactive, rise, fall, unimodal) validating the approach
Novel hallucination snowballing (HS) metric capturing both severity and propagation distance that benefits the broader community
Thorough appendix with hyperparameter sensitivity analysis and comprehensive experimental settings supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (temperature scaling, attention-based token selection, masking) are standard techniques; core contribution is problem identification rather than novel mechanisms

Unclear theoretical justification for why visual relay tokens prevent propagation; Equation 1 contextualizes visual tokens with instructions, potentially reintroducing the text-bias problem the method aims to solve
Insufficient explanation of why existing single-agent hallucination methods (MemVR, VISTA, DeCo, TAME) perform worse than baseline in multi-agent settings, raising fairness concerns about comparisons
Modest individual component contributions (Table 6: 0.2-2.0% impact); unclear whether gains come from specific mechanism design or simply additional visual information
Limited scope: evaluation restricted to visual QA tasks; other hallucination types (spatial, attribute, relational) unexplored; single-turn scenarios show minimal improvement (Figure 7)
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, significance tests, or multiple seeds reported; some improvements are modest (0.5-1.5% on MME/MMBench)
Key-Norm approximation shows degradation vs. attention scores (Table 7) and uses ad-hoc 3×3 buffer; only ~70% overlap with original selection raises approximation quality concerns
Generalization limitations: restricted to 7B-34B models, truncated analysis at 20 turns, only tested on distributed MAS architectures, parameters tuned on circular structure

strengths: Novel problem formulation: Identifies and formalizes multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing, distinguishing between intrinsic hallucination and propagation—an important failure mode not addressed by single-agent methods
Thorough diagnostic analysis: Comprehensive layer-wise, token-wise attention analysis across 6 diverse VLMs clearly motivates the solution through ablations showing ~3x impact of unimodal tokens

Extensive experimental validation: Tested on 10 base models (7B-34B), 8 benchmarks, 4 MAS structures, plus multi-image and video scenarios; consistent improvements (2.4-3.8% comprehensive, 4%+ hallucination-specific)
Model-agnostic and practical: Lightweight method works across diverse architectures without retraining, includes Key-Norm alternative for Flash Attention models

Comprehensive ablations and analysis: Detailed ablation studies, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis (Tables 12-14), efficiency analysis showing reasonable overhead, case studies demonstrating effectiveness
Proposed HS metric: Introduces quantitative measure of multi-agent hallucination propagation with robustness validation (94% inter-judge agreement within 10%)
Strong reproducibility: Code availability promised, detailed experimental settings, specified hyperparameters, implementation details well-documented
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Unimodal token selection and attention reallocation via temperature scaling/masking are straightforward applications of existing techniques; primary contribution is problem formulation rather than methodology

Insufficient causal analysis: Establishes correlation between visual attention reduction and hallucination but not causality; lacks theoretical explanation for why unimodal tokens preserve visual information or how visual flow prevents propagation

Modest improvements on standard benchmarks: Only 1-3% improvement on comprehensive benchmarks (MME, MMBench, MM-Vet) with 8.1-13.4% computational overhead; may not justify practical adoption for general tasks
Key-Norm alternative is less principled: For Flash Attention models, resort to L2-norm workaround with ad-hoc 3×3 buffer tuning; reduces confidence in generalizability to future model architectures
Hyperparameter tuning requirements: Introduces 4 hyperparameters (ω, τ, α₁, α₂) requiring manual setting; unclear how to select these for new models/tasks; no principled selection strategy provided
Training pipeline ambiguity: Table 10 shows fine-tuning requirement contradicting 'training-free' claims; unclear data requirements and practical feasibility for practitioners
Missing failure case analysis: No discussion of when method underperforms, which hallucination types are hardest to mitigate, or scenarios where visual relay tokens don't help
Limited comparison fairness: Compared methods designed for single-agent settings; not surprising they underperform in multi-agent context; lacks comparison to dedicated multi-agent approaches

Evaluation methodology concerns: HS metric relies on GPT-4 judge introducing potential biases; connection between HS score reduction and original metric improvements unclear; some benchmarks (CHAIR, POPE) may not capture multi-agent phenomena
Scope limitations: Analysis primarily focuses on circular MAS structure; generalizability to hierarchical/specialized-role systems and other collaboration paradigms unclear

strengths: Novel problem identification: Multi-agent visual hallucination snowballing is a genuine failure mode specific to VLM-based MAS that distinguishes intrinsic hallucination from propagation

Rigorous empirical analysis: Comprehensive turn-, layer-, and token-wise attention analyses with well-designed ablation studies across five token subsets; clear finding that unimodal tokens in middle layers are 2-3× more important
Comprehensive experimental validation: 8 primary + 4 augmented benchmarks, 4 MAS structures, 10 models (7B-34B), showing consistent 2.4-3.8% improvements with larger models benefiting even more (>4%)
Model-agnostic design: Works across diverse VLM architectures without model-specific tuning; efficient with only 8-13% additional latency and 4-12% computational overhead

Practical significance: Identifies an important challenge for real-world multi-agent VLM systems and provides a working solution; improvements scale to larger models suggesting latent capacity unlocking

Strong methodological execution: Proper comparisons with 5 existing methods, novel HS metric capturing hallucination propagation, ablation studies validating each component, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis
Good auxiliary analyses: Impact of agent turns showing ViF maintains performance while baselines degrade, correction capability on adversarial inputs, cross-judge consistency validation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core components (attention-based token selection, temperature scaling, mask-based attention reallocation) are individually standard; main contribution is identifying which tokens to select rather than novel techniques

Insufficient theoretical justification: Why unimodal tokens specifically preserve visual evidence is only empirically demonstrated, not mechanistically explained; no formal analysis of hallucination snowballing or proof of mitigation

Heuristic design choices: Selection via unimodal attention peak (parameter ω) is somewhat ad-hoc; reallocation direction motivated only by observation; Eq. 1's token length maintenance strategy not well justified; multiple hyperparameters requiring tuning

Evaluation concerns: Modest improvements on some benchmarks (e.g., MMBench: 0.5-1.4%); HS metric relies on GPT-5 as external judge (unclear if released model); comparison methods are single-agent approaches applied to MAS rather than designed for it
Single-agent case shows minimal improvement: ViF provides little benefit at turn 1 (equivalent to single agent), limiting impact claims for fundamental hallucination reduction

Limited scope and generalization: Experiments use specific linear context growth MAS strategy; assumes dual-agent multi-round collaboration; generalization to other multi-agent tasks beyond VQA (collaborative reasoning, planning) unexplored; primarily tested on VQA and hallucination detection

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Limited explanation for why larger models benefit more; why circular structure suffers most only intuitively discussed; no analysis of failure cases or when ViF is less effective

Method-to-claim mismatch: Requires two-stage training (pre-training + instruction tuning), somewhat contradicting 'model-agnostic' framing; Key-Norm alternative shows >30% token difference from attention-based selection
